sections.html:
Three options face a Yuma seller: hire an agent, handle it privately, or accept cash for the house in its present state. All three finish at a Yuma County title company, followed by a recorded deed and a sales affidavit.

Many sellers here are military households tied to Marine Corps Air Station Yuma and Yuma Proving Ground, or owners who live elsewhere for part of the year. An estimated 70,000 to over 85,000 out-of-state visitors spend the winter in Yuma. For any of these sellers the fastest path is the one where title, taxes and permits are already settled.

Line up these papers before you ask for offers:

  • Lender payoff letters and the Yuma County parcel number
  • Your latest tax statement and proof the 2026 first half is paid
  • Permit records for patios, pools, garages or an accessory dwelling
  • Tenant leases and, if the house is in a revitalization area, any rental inspection certification

Yuma has 105,227 residents, up from 95,548 at the 2020 census, and owners occupy 66.8% of homes. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $230,000. Median gross rent is $1,114, median household income is $65,482 and there are 39,110 households averaging 2.49 people. The city covers 120.67 square miles, so lots and neighborhoods vary a good deal. Compare your house with recent sales close to it rather than with the city median.

If you are selling a second home or live out of state for part of the year, set up a signing by mail or with a notary near you and give the title company a local contact for access. A cash sale can often be arranged without you returning to Yuma.

Agriculture and the military anchor the local economy. Yuma County grows more than 175 crops, with lettuce the largest.

Three school districts touch most listings:

  • Yuma Union High School District, the high school district for the city
  • Yuma Elementary District One, which covers central and eastern Yuma
  • The Crane district, which covers the northwest part of the city

Verify the district for your exact address before advertising, since buyers ask about attendance boundaries.

Intense sun and long summers wear on roofs, coatings and cooling equipment, and buyers know it. Yuma gets just 3.36 inches of rain in an average year, and temperatures reach 100 degrees or higher on 117 days a year, mostly from April through October.

A roof, a cooling system or a water heater in its final years deserves a quote or an inspection before you list. If the property has mature citrus or other landscaping, expect buyers to ask about its condition.

New construction, remodels, and electrical, mechanical and plumbing work generally need a permit and inspection from the City of Yuma Building Safety Division. Minor work such as fencing, painting and small repairs is often exempt, and staff can tell you which is which.

Residential reviews normally take 5 work days and commercial reviews 15 work days. Ask for an inspection before 3 p.m. and it is scheduled the next business day. A Certificate of Occupancy comes only after the required inspections pass. File applications on the Development Portal.

The 2024 IBC, IRC, IEBC and IPMC apply to new permit applications. The city's Permit-Ready Plans Program offers pre-reviewed home designs, including three pre-approved accessory dwelling unit plans. That helps if you want a buyer to know an ADU is feasible.

A tenant-occupied house inside a city revitalization area comes with extra rules. The Neighborhood Services Rental Inspection Program inspects every rental unit in those neighborhoods against the housing code in Chapter 138 of the Yuma Code of Ordinances.

When inspectors find problems, the owner is asked to make repairs, and follow-up visits confirm the fixes before the unit is certified. Inspectors need the tenant's signed access form, though the tenant does not have to be home, and the landlord or property manager can accompany the inspector.

Ask Neighborhood Services whether your address sits in a revitalization area and whether it holds a current certification. Any buyer planning to keep the tenant will ask about certification. The Arizona Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies as well, so check your lease and notice duties before you promise a closing date.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and penalties
sections.html:
Two county offices handle your tax: the Treasurer collects it and the Assessor sets the value.

InstallmentDue dateDelinquent after 5 p.m.
First halfOctober 1November 1
Second halfMarch 1May 1

A date that falls on a weekend moves to the next business day, and the second half for 2026 taxes is listed as May 3, 2027.

A late payment accrues simple interest of 16% a year, prorated by the month. If you pay both installments by December 31, no interest is assessed on the first half. On January 1, 2027, 2025 delinquent taxes pick up a 5% penalty. To stay out of the tax lien sale set for February 18, 2027, pay unpaid 2025 taxes by 5 p.m. on February 17, 2027.

After a sale, the new owner should confirm the name and mailing address with the Assessor's Office before bills go out in August. The Assessor is at 197 S. Main Street, phone 928-373-6040. To contest a valuation, file a Petition for Review of Valuation; the appeal addresses value only and not how large the bill is. Your title company will request a payoff so tax due is paid at closing.

The Yuma County Recorder's Office takes deeds at 298 South Main Street, weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The phone is 928-373-6020. You can also mail the document or use a third-party e-recording provider that serves the county.

A signed Affidavit of Property Value must go with the deed unless an exemption applies. A.R.S. 11-1133 has both parties certify the sale date, total consideration, financing type, parcel number and whether the house is owner-occupied or rented, and the recorder must refuse a deed without a complete affidavit. On the form, the sale date means the day the contract was signed. If you pay by mail, call the office first for the current fee schedule.

In practice the title company handles the trip. It searches the record, gathers payoffs, sets up the signing and files the deed for you, so you only need to bring photo ID and your lender and tenant paperwork.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax on a Yuma house?
faqs.a: The Treasurer collects, and the Assessor sets the value. A first-half payment is late once 5 p.m. passes on November 1, and a second-half payment once it passes on May 1.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss the Yuma County tax deadlines?
faqs.a: Simple interest of 16% a year builds up by the month. Delinquent 2025 taxes add a 5% penalty on January 1, 2027, and a parcel left unpaid can go to the tax lien sale on February 18, 2027.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for work on my Yuma house?
faqs.a: Usually yes for new construction, remodels, and electrical, mechanical or plumbing work. The Building Safety Division reviews residential plans in about 5 work days. Call before you start so staff can tell you whether your project needs a permit.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Yuma?
faqs.a: Take it to 298 South Main Street, Yuma, AZ 85364, or let the title company file it. The phone for hours and fees is 928-373-6020. Include an Affidavit of Property Value or note an exemption.

Rentals in the city's revitalization areas are inspected under Chapter 138 of the Yuma Code of Ordinances. Inspectors need the tenant's signed access form, and the owner repairs any problems before certification.
